extracted.intended_audience: allergists, ophthalmologists, pediatricians, and clinicians managing ocular allergy
extracted.subtask_description: Clinical review summarizing classification, pathophysiology, diagnostic features, and therapeutic options for the various forms of allergic conjunctivitis (SAC, PAC, VKC, AKC, contact allergy, GPC), with pediatric considerations. Useful as guidance for clinicians evaluating and managing patients with ocular allergy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusive classification of allergic conjunctivitis
rubrics_metrics.description: Allergic conjunctivitis is an inclusive term that encompasses seasonal allergic conjunctivitis (SAC), perennial allergic conjunctivitis (PAC), vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC), atopic keratoconjunctivitis (AKC), contact allergy, and giant papillary conjunctivitis (GPC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AKC and VKC have clinical and pathophysiological features quite different from SAC and PAC. Contact-lens or prosthesis-associated GPC should not be considered true allergic diseases but chronic micro-trauma–related disorders managed with ophthalmology/contact-lens expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary clinical diagnosis with supportive laboratory testing
rubrics_metrics.description: The diagnosis of ocular allergy is primarily clinical, based on history and characteristic signs/symptoms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allergists can perform skin testing (scratch/intradermal) or in-vitro tests for specific IgE antibodies to support diagnosis and help differentiate intrinsic and extrinsic forms; these tests are helpful for guiding treatment but clinical assessment is central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core symptoms/signs for SAC and PAC
rubrics_metrics.description: SAC and PAC diagnostic features consist of itching, redness (conjunctival injection), and swelling (chemosis); itching is fairly consistent; corneal involvement is rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SAC is seasonal (airborne pollens, spring/summer), PAC occurs year-round (perennial allergens). Redness tends to be mild-moderate; chemosis may be moderate and more prominent than expected for redness.

rubrics_metrics.name: VKC diagnostic and severity features
rubrics_metrics.description: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis is a chronic allergic inflammation more common in warm climates and young people, often with nonspecific hyperreactivity to wind/dust/sunlight and negative skin/IgE tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: VKC has palpebral, limbal, and mixed forms; characteristic signs include giant papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva, Trantas dots, tenacious mucous discharge, photophobia, and potential corneal involvement (punctate keratitis, plaques, shield ulcers) that can lead to scarring and visual loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: AKC diagnostic and distinguishing features
rubrics_metrics.description: Atopic keratoconjunctivitis is a bilateral chronic inflammatory ocular surface disease associated with atopic dermatitis and involves both IgE-mediated and Th1/Th2 immune mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Features include eyelid eczematous lesions, conjunctival injection/chemosis, possible giant papillae, conjunctival scarring, Trantas dots, and risk of atopic cataracts; AKC can persist throughout life (unlike VKC which often resolves by age 20).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact allergy (allergic contact dermatitis) criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Contact allergy is a type-IV delayed hypersensitivity response (non–IgE-mediated) occurring via sensitization and elicitation phases mediated by memory T-lymphocytes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical allergens include small chemicals (poison ivy/oak, neomycin, nickel, latex). Reactions may appear on eyelids/periocular skin and conjunctiva, peaking 2–5 days after re-exposure; treatment consists of withdrawing and avoiding the allergen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Giant papillary conjunctivitis (GPC) characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: GPC is papillary hypertrophy of the superior tarsal conjunctiva similar in appearance to vernal conjunctivitis but typically without significant corneal involvement and is not a systemic allergic disease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caused by inert stimuli (contact lenses, prostheses, sutures); incidence decreases with disposable lenses. Removing the irritative stimulus leads to resolution. Mechanisms include protein deposits (possible antigenicity) and mechanical trauma releasing mediators (e.g., CXCL8, TNF-α).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathophysiology overview as diagnostic/therapeutic guide
rubrics_metrics.description: Allergic conjunctivitis pathogenesis involves IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation for many forms, but Th2 lymphocytes, eosinophils, neutrophils, cytokines, chemokines, adhesion molecules, growth factors, and other pathways variably contribute across entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding the differing mediators and mechanisms across syndromes explains variability in clinical features, diagnostic test results, and therapeutic responses; the review suggests a mechanism-based classification would be desirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-line nonpharmacologic management: avoidance and tear substitutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoidance of offending antigens is the primary behavioral modification; artificial tear substitutes provide barrier/dilution/flush functions on the ocular surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoidance may be difficult because of large ocular surface exposure to airborne allergens; artificial tears help dilute allergens and inflammatory mediators and support conjunctival mucosal defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical antihistamines: rapid but short-lived symptomatic relief
rubrics_metrics.description: Topical H1 antihistamines (e.g., levocabastine) rapidly relieve itching and redness by competitively and reversibly blocking histamine receptors but have short duration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent dosing up to 4 times daily may be necessary; topical antihistamines do not affect other proinflammatory mediators (prostaglandins, leukotrienes) and may be irritating with prolonged use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decongestant-containing drops: short-term erythema control with risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Combination decongestant/antihistamine drops reduce erythema via vasoconstriction and provide short-term symptom relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adverse effects include burning/stinging, mydriasis, and rebound hyperemia (conjunctivitis medicamentosa) with chronic use; suitable only short-term and contraindicated in narrow-angle glaucoma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mast cell stabilizers: prophylactic use requiring loading period
rubrics_metrics.description: Mast cell stabilizers prevent mast cell degranulation and are used prophylactically to prevent symptoms; they do not relieve established symptoms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require a loading period (must be applied before antigen exposure); poor compliance due to loading requirement is a drawback; suitable for more severe/recurring forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-modal anti-allergic agents as drugs of choice for immediate relief
rubrics_metrics.description: Newer multi-modal agents (olopatadine, ketotifen, azelastine, epinastine, bepostatine) combine antihistamine, mast-cell stabilization, and anti-inflammatory effects and are becoming drugs of choice for immediate symptomatic relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ketotifen inhibits eosinophil activation and leukotriene/cytokine release; azelastine blocks H1 and PAF and ICAM-1 expression; epinastine affects H1/H2 and has anti-inflammatory effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: NSAIDs as adjuncts for hyperemia and pruritus
rubrics_metrics.description: Topical NSAIDs can be used as additive drugs to reduce conjunctival hyperemia and pruritus mediated by prostaglandins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider as adjunct when appropriate; not first-line monotherapy for allergic inflammatory control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corticosteroids for severe or refractory disease with safety precautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Topical corticosteroids are the most potent pharmacologic agents for severe variants and acute/chronic forms but have significant ocular adverse effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit courses to short durations (up to 2 weeks) when possible; adverse effects include delayed wound healing, secondary infection, elevated intraocular pressure, and cataract formation. For longer treatment, perform baseline and periodic eye exams including cataract assessment and intraocular pressure measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allergen-specific immunotherapy indications and caveats
rubrics_metrics.description: Allergen-specific immunotherapy is effective for patients with allergic rhinoconjunctivitis who have specific IgE to allergens; the objective is to induce clinical tolerance and modify immune responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therapy can reduce specific IgE and increase IgG4/IgA via IL-10 and TGF-β1; immune-response measures do not reliably predict clinical efficacy. Immunotherapy can cause systemic reactions varying by allergen and method. Traditionally subcutaneous; sublingual (SLIT) is gaining use but requires further evaluation specifically for ocular symptom control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systemic (oral) antihistamines considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Second-generation oral antihistamines are recommended over first-generation due to reduced somnolence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Second-generation agents can induce ocular drying that may impair tear-film barrier and potentially worsen ocular symptoms; concomitant topical eye drops may improve ocular symptom control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intranasal corticosteroids: effective for nasal, inconsistent for ocular symptoms
rubrics_metrics.description: Intranasal corticosteroids are highly effective for nasal allergic rhinitis symptoms but evidence for efficacy in treating ocular symptoms is inconsistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on intranasal steroids alone for ocular symptom control; evaluate patient response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pediatric-specific considerations and referral thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: Allergic conjunctivitis is common in children, often with other atopic diseases; AKC and VKC are less common but potentially more severe in pediatrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symptoms include bilateral itching, tearing, mucoid discharge, redness, mild eyelid edema, and chemosis. Pediatric ophthalmology involvement is recommended for severe cases to avoid preventable vision loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation for mechanism-based reclassification
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the varied mediators and pathways across allergic ocular disorders, a new classification system derived from pathophysiological mechanisms is desirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mechanism-based classification may better reflect diagnostic features and predict response to treatment than the current inclusive/clinical categories.
